Commentary.Commentary: We are back for the all-important run chase. The umpires are back out in the middle and so are the players of South Africa. It will be the southpaw duo of Abhishek Sharma and Ishan Kishan to open the innings for India. Aiden Markram is taking the new ball himself with Kishan on strike. Let's play...
... The Run Chase ...

Will 187 be enough? The game is nicely poised at the halfway mark, and the Proteas will hope that the late momentum with the bat translates into early success with the ball. For India, the focus will be firmly on Abhishek Sharma. With three ducks in the tournament so far, he will be feeling the pressure to deliver. An intriguing second half of the game awaits us. Stick around!

Momentum swings at the death - Varun has been a banker for India in the middle overs, not just in this tournament but in the build-up to the event as well. However, on the night he was put under real pressure, that pushed India into uncharted territory. After finally breaking the 97-run stand between Dewald Brevis and David Miller and removing both set batters, India did manage to claw their way back into the contest. Jasprit Bumrah's return helped the home side tighten the screws and regain control, but Stubbs came through to provide the finishing kick.

India strike first, Proteas respond - The Proteas' top order was blown away inside the powerplay by Arshdeep Singh and Jasprit Bumrah, with the ball stopping a touch early on and the batters not quite giving themselves enough time to adjust. Reduced to 20/3, David Miller stepped up and began the repair work. A few crisp boundaries settled the nerves and helped South Africa finish the powerplay on a positive note. That momentum carried into the middle phase as Dewald Brevis joined in and the pair took down Varun Chakaravarthy.

South Africa end up with 187 - 20 runs off the final over and South Africa finish on a real high. Looking at the way their innings lost steam after David Miller perished, one wondered whether the innings would fizzle out, but Tristan Stubbs has helped them finish with a flourish. The Proteas will walk into the break with a bit of momentum, while India will be a bit disappointed at the finish.

SIX! Yes, he can! Stubbs goes bang-bang to end the first innings. Shortish length yet again from Pandya, over off stump, Tristan Stubbs leans across and hoicks the pull behind square leg for a biggie. 20 runs off the final over and South Africa finish with 187/7 on the board.

Commentary.Commentary: The national anthems are done, and we are all set for the action to begin. Suryakumar Yadav has gathered his men for a huddle with the skipper doing all the talking. It will be the left-hand, right-hand combination of Quinton de Kock and Aiden Markram to open the innings for South Africa. Arshdeep Singh will open the attack for India. It will be interesting to see if the left-arm seamer gets any movement through the air. Arshdeep to Markram with a slip in place. The wait is over, and away we go...

The giant flags have been unfurled, and it is now time for the national anthems. Ravi Shastri expects a crowd of over 80,000 to turn up tonight in Ahmedabad. It is a sea of blue as you would expect. Suryakumar Yadav and Aiden Markram lead their troops out, along with the mascots. It will be the national anthem of South Africa first, followed by that of the home side.

Important to follow good habits - The Indian skipper, Suryakumar Yadav says he would have batted first as well, but he is not too disappointed with the outcome of the toss. He mentions there was a little bit in the wicket early on during the Netherlands game and hopes that is the case tonight as well. Tells that it is a big game and he sees it as a good occasion for everyone to show their character. SKY hopes the team can entertain the crowd. Believes that although there are 3 games in the Super 8s, they need to land that punch from ball one and bring good energy to the field. Informs that they are going with the same team as the last game. Admits that it is a bit harsh on Axar Patel, who misses out but it is a tactical call.

Ready for the challenge - The captain of South Africa, Aiden Markram says they will bat first as it looks like a really good cricket, a little drier than they thought and a bit tacky too. Reckons the boys are in good form, confident and are ready to turn up. Mentions that they are fortunate to play here multiple times and reckons they are playing on a black soil wicket today. Informs that they have made four changes, with all the front-line players back in the team.

South Africa (Playing XI) - Aiden Markram (C), Quinton de Kock (WK), Ryan Rickelton, Dewald Brevis, David Miller (In for Jason Smith), Tristan Stubbs, Marco Jansen (In for Kwena Maphaka), Corbin Bosch, Kagiso Rabada, Keshav Maharaj (In for George Linde) and Lungi Ngidi (In for Anrich Nortje).

India (Unchanged Playing XI) - Abhishek Sharma, Ishan Kishan (WK), Tilak Varma, Suryakumar Yadav (C), Hardik Pandya, Shivam Dube, Rinku Singh, Washington Sundar, Arshdeep Singh, Varun Chakaravarthy and Jasprit Bumrah.

TOSS - Time for the coin to go up in Ahmedabad. Suryakumar Yadav and Aiden Markram have made their way out to the centre, accompanied by match referee Ranjan Madugalle. Ravi Shastri gets the crowd going as he belts out the introduction of the three men who matter at the toss. 'Tails' is the call from Markram, and he gets it right. South Africa elect to BAT first.

PITCH REPORT - Ravi Shastri is out in the middle. He shares that the temperature is hovering in the low 30s, 32 degrees Celsius to be exact. Tells that the boundary dimensions read 64 and 67 metres square, with 72 metres straight down the ground. Shaun Pollock joins him, and he informs that this is pitch number five, a black soil surface. Mentions that this is the same wicket where India played South Africa in a T20I in December last year, in which India scored 231 and in reply, South Africa posted 201. Pollock adds that the average first innings score at this venue is 192, the highest among the Indian grounds hosting matches at this World Cup. He also points out that there is a little less grass compared to some of the earlier games here, with a few more visible cracks on the surface. Even so, it looks like a good wicket that should hold up well throughout the contest. With the river close to the ground, Pollock does wonder whether dew could become a factor later in the evening.

Chaos in the chase - In case you stepped out after a dominant first half from Sri Lanka in Pallekele, you are in for a surprise. Chasing 147, Sri Lanka have been bowled out for just 95 in 16.4 overs. Yes, you read that right. What looked like a straightforward chase never took off, largely due to a self-implosion from the Lankan batters. England have come away with a 51-run win, who would have thought, especially after the struggles right throughout with the bat for Harry Brook and his men.

Bowlers in the spotlight - Ahmedabad may have seen plenty of runs, but as the saying goes, batters win you games, but bowlers win you tournaments. So let us take a look at the men who could tilt this contest with the ball. Varun Chakaravarthy is India's premier weapon in the middle overs, especially between overs 7 and 16, heading into the Super 8s. Since the last World Cup, he has taken the most wickets (54) in this phase. For South Africa, Lungi Ngidi and Keshav Maharaj have caused India plenty of trouble in recent T20Is. Both are among the top three wicket takers against India in the format since 2022.

Runs versus restraint - South Africa's batting has been one of the standout features of the tournament so far. They scored at 9.4 runs per over in the group stage, the second best in the competition, and maintained a batting average of 39.4, which was the third highest. Up against them is arguably the most disciplined bowling attack of the group phase. India conceded just 6.9 runs per over, the best economy rate in the tournament, and also had the second-best bowling strike rate of 13.

Clash of the Titans - Hello and a warm welcome, everyone. A blockbuster clash in Ahmedabad awaits us as two heavyweights of the tournament lock horns. Both sides sailed through the group stage unbeaten, but all of that now counts for little. The Super 8s bring a fresh start and zero margin for error. One slip here and you immediately find yourself playing catch-up in a short and unforgiving phase.
... MATCH DAY ...

The sequel nobody wants to miss - Let us rewind to June 2024. Kensington Oval, Barbados. South Africa were cruising in the T20 World Cup final, one hand on the trophy, when Hardik Pandya, Jasprit Bumrah and Arshdeep Singh produced a spell for the ages to rip it away and leave the Proteas heartbroken. Fast forward to 2026 and the two heavyweights collide again, this time in Match 3 of the Super 8s at the Narendra Modi Stadium in Ahmedabad. And this is no ordinary Super 8 group, with West Indies and Zimbabwe also in the mix, two other unbeaten group toppers, this has quickly become the tournament's toughest pool. Perfect group stages, different paths - Both sides arrive unbeaten. South Africa swept past New Zealand, Canada and UAE comfortably, but their defining moment came in that unforgettable clash against Afghanistan - a double Super Over epic that will live long in World Cup folklore. India, too, topped their group with four wins, brushing aside Netherlands and Namibia and dominating Pakistan, but they had to dig deep in their opener against USA, rescued by Suryakumar Yadav's match-winning 84 off 49. India's firepower - India may not have hit absolute top gear yet, but they have found match-winners at every turn. Ishan Kishan smashed a blistering 77 against Pakistan on a slow Colombo surface, Shivam Dube hammered 66 off 31 against Netherlands, and Hardik Pandya has delivered crucial all-round impact time and again. Add Rinku Singh's finishing prowess and India's tally of 40 sixes - the most in the group stage, with Kishan contributing 11 and the batting depth looks formidable. The bowling have been pretty sharp. Varun Chakravarthy has been outstanding with nine wickets, bossing the middle overs, Axar Patel has been reliable (and likely returns after being rested), while Bumrah and Arshdeep have been clinical both up front and at the death. A few warning signs - Yet there are cracks to address. The No.1 ranked T20I batter Abhishek Sharma has three ducks and is yet to score. A concerning pattern has also emerged when Tilak Varma and SKY bat together, both striking under 125 in recent games, particularly struggling against off-spin. India are scoring at just 6.23 against off-spinners, with an average of 13.25, numbers only better than Nepal and Oman. Add nine dropped catches - the second most in the tournament and there are clear areas to tighten up. Markram's men mean business - South Africa have been equally impressive. Aiden Markram has led from the front with two fifties, including a superb 86 against New Zealand, while Ryan Rickelton boasts the highest strike rate in the squad (minimum 10 balls faced). Quinton de Kock has quietly crossed 100 runs, anchoring things smartly at the top. Dewald Brevis, though, is yet to truly ignite this campaign - something that will be on the management's mind but he will take confidence from the white-ball tour of India late last year, where he played a couple of impactful knocks and showed exactly the kind of damage he can inflict on this very opposition. Tristan Stubbs and David Miller continue to finish strongly - Stubbs already a hero for that last-ball six in the first Super Over against Afghanistan. Proteas pace battery firing - Their pace unit has been nothing short of lethal. Lungi Ngidi, Marco Jansen and Corbin Bosch have combined for 20 wickets, with both Ngidi and Jansen registering four-fers in the tournament. Interestingly, Kagiso Rabada has managed just two wickets in four games so far, while Anrich Nortje returned in the final league fixture to pick up a couple himself, creating a healthy selection dilemma ahead of this clash. The real weapon, though, has been their clever use of off-pace deliveries, consistently unsettling batters at the death and in the Powerplay as well. Add to that the spin options of Keshav Maharaj, George Linde and skipper Aiden Markram, particularly valuable against India's left-hand-heavy batting unit and South Africa possess a bowling attack that is both varied and tactically flexible. Team Form (Last 5 T20Is, latest result first) - India - WWWWW | South Africa - WWWWL. Venue trends and historical edge - Historically, India lead 5-2 in T20 World Cups, though South Africa won their most recent meeting before the 2024 final, in 2022, with Ngidi starring. At this venue, pacers have enjoyed greater success than spinners, and with an average first-innings score of 192, another high-scoring encounter seems likely. South Africa have already adapted well here with wins batting first and chasing under lights, while India also defended successfully in Ahmedabad in their last outing. Built for a thriller - With night conditions favouring batters and two explosive line-ups in top form, this promises to be a heavyweight showdown. The ghosts of Barbados linger, but in Ahmedabad, a new chapter awaits and if history is any guide, expect drama, big hits and a finish worthy of a World Cup classic.
